title: My Team Was Doing Their Jobs Perfectly. The Problem Was Me
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder's confessional piece traces her realization that her leadership style created an organizational bottleneck disguised as high standards. When her team completed all assigned tasks but five critical action items sat unmoved because they required her approval, Mulder confronted an uncomfortable truth: she had built a company where everything important ran through her personally. She had conflated indispensability with leadership effectiveness, keeping decision-making authority while distributing responsibility, which exhausted her team and capped organizational growth at her personal capacity. She distinguishes between responsibility (doing work) and ownership (protecting outcomes with real authority), revealing how her "hands-on" approach prevented subordinates from developing into decision-makers. The turning point was reframing from what needs to happen to what needs to happen without me, forcing an honest audit of whether her centralized control served quality or her identity. Mulder now focuses on building bench strength rather than bottlenecks, asking regularly whether her leadership develops independent leaders or reinforces dependency. She acknowledges that high performers sense and resent these constraints, and the best ones eventually leave.
points: Bottleneck leadership masquerades as quality control; a CEO who insists on being the decision-maker on everything creates organizational ceiling that prevents team growth and decision-making authority distribution.

The identity trap: confusing indispensability with leadership value. Moving from being needed to building bench strength requires facing uncomfortable questions about who you are beyond your central role.

Responsibility without ownership exhausts teams; true delegation requires not only assigning tasks but transferring real authority and decision-making power so team members protect outcomes, not just execute.

The question reframe from what needs to get done to what needs to get done without me forces leaders to examine whether centralized decision-making is actually about standards or about identity protection.
High performers sense and resent organizational bottlenecks; the best team members eventually leave companies where growth is capped by a single person's capacity.
quotes: I had built a company where everything important ran through one person. And that person was me. Being indispensable felt like being valuable. Being the answer to everything felt like being a good leader.

Every time you stepped in when you shouldn't have, you reinforced it. Every time you handled something because it was faster than training someone, you reinforced it. Every time you kept a piece of the business in your head instead of in a system, you reinforced it.
Being indispensable and being a good leader are not the same thing. They are almost opposites. A good leader builds people who can move without them.
The real work isn't operational. The solving part has nothing to do with delegation plans or org charts or the right system. The real work is identity.

There is a difference between giving someone responsibility and giving someone ownership. Responsibility means they do the work. Ownership means they protect the outcome and they have the real authority to do it.
Instead of asking what needs to get done, I started asking what needs to get done without me. That reframe sounds small. It isn't.

Your highest performers feel an empty bench. They feel the weight of a company where too much depends on too few people. They feel the gap where leadership should be developing.” Archived from Summer Mulder Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
